newsitem.title: HONG KONG: Bondholders miffed by possible Riaupulp redemption.
newsitem.headline: Bondholders miffed by possible Riaupulp redemption.

text.p: A reported plan by Indonesian pulp and paper company Riaupulp to sell assets in a power plant and a chemical plant could cost bondholders millions of dollars, market sources said Monday.
Riau Andalan Pulp is 98.9 percent owned by Asia Pacific Resources International Holdings.
Another APRIL group member, Inti Indorayon Utama, is expected to acquire Riaupulp's chemical assets if Indorayon shareholders approve. Riaupulp power assets also are on the block, sources said.

Indenture forms on US$300 million of outstanding Yankee bonds of Riapulp unit Rapp International Finance oblige Riaupulp to retire all of its oustanding secured debt at 101 percent of the principal amount if collateral sales exceed 25 percent of the book value of the collateral, sources said.
The obligation could also affect US$250 million in outstanding secured bank debt, they said.
Some market sources said that until recently they were not aware of the redemption option on the Yankee bonds that would be triggered by the planned sale of assets in the two plants.
They complained that the option was not adequately highlighted in the bond's prospectus.
"In essence, there's a (redemption) into what was supposed to be a non-callable bond," said Keith Nilsson, associate of Asia research at Bankers Trust in Hong Kong.
"Even if they have the call option, they should not excercise it," said a bond trader at a European bank in Singapore, adding "it's a question of morality here, and ethics."
For holders of the Yankee bonds maturing in 2000 and 2005, the redemption could mean millions of dollars in losses.
Traders said US$100 million of 11.5 percent bonds due in 2000 were trading at 105 on January 10, and another US$200 million of 13.25 percent bonds due in 2005 were trading at 111.
If called at 101, as stipulated in the "mandatory redemption" clause, holders of the bonds would stand to lose a total of US$24 million, sources said.
Some sources charged that there is no economic rationale for the asset sale beyond triggering the bond redemption.
"Nobody expects the company to do an asset sale kind of a thing unless it is in dire financial straits. There is no economic reason for them to behave this way," the bond trader said.
Sources say an investor conference call has been arranged with the company and Salomon Brothers, lead manager of the Yankee issue, to be held at 0100 GMT Tuesday.
Reports of the teleconference could not be immediatly confirmed.
